Caspian tern (Hydroprogne caspia) is a large, cosmopolitan species known for its conspicuous nesting colonies and relatively slow life history pace compared to smaller charadriiforms. Freshly laid eggs, which average 6.45 centimeters in length and 4.46 centimeters in width, have an estimated fresh weight of approximately 67.1 grams, a value derived from the standard ellipsoid formula for avian eggs. Upon hatching, the altricial chicks display a modest wet weight at birth of 60 grams [Wwb = 60 grams], a mass that reflects the substantial energetic reserves provided by the yolk and albumen within the sizable egg. Incubation periods under controlled conditions have been documented at 27.2 days [ab = 27.2 days] when the eggs are maintained at a stable temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a thermal regime often considered the optimal artificial incubation temperature for many large tern species. This incubation duration is somewhat longer than that observed in smaller congeners, likely due to the larger egg volume and the associated thermal mass, which buffers against rapid temperature fluctuations during the attentive periods of the parent birds.

Following the nesting phase, the developmental trajectory of the chick proceeds through several key stages, many of which are influenced by the thermal environment typical of the breeding grounds. Within the active metabolic temperature range characteristic of the species, which is around 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], the time since birth at fledging is observed at approximately 37 days [tx = approximately 37 days]. This milestone, marked by the achievement of sustained flight and the development of flight feathers of sufficient length, occurs at an age quite typical for a bird of this size. The fledgling remains dependent on its parents for several weeks thereafter, refining its foraging skills before achieving true independence. The transition from a sedentary nestling, which is brooded extensively in the first week to ten days, to an active juvenile capable of short flights is a period of rapid physiological and muscular development. The downy chick of the first week is gradually replaced by the definitive juvenile plumage, a process that demands significant nutritional input from the provisioning adults and is sensitive to local food availability.

Puberty in Caspian terns, defined here as the age at attainment of sexual maturity and the onset of gonadal activity, is reached relatively early in the species' life cycle. Under the same thermal regime typical of the species' active metabolism of approximately 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], the time since birth at puberty is estimated at 111 days [tp = 111 days]. This value falls within the range of 33 to 39 days often cited in the literature for this parameter, though a more conservative figure of 111 days accounts for individual variation and the energetic challenges of the post-fledging period. This relatively rapid maturation allows young birds to prospect for breeding territories and assess colony dynamics during their first summer, even if they do not breed successfully until a later year. The onset of full reproductive viability does not, however, translate into immediate breeding activity. Most individuals delay their first reproductive attempt until they have accumulated sufficient foraging experience and fat reserves, a strategy common among long-lived seabirds that prioritizes adult survival over early reproduction.

The first successful breeding event for a Caspian tern typically occurs after a prolonged period of juvenile and subadult development. The time since birth at first brood is documented at 1095 days [tR = 1095 days] at the species' typical active metabolic temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This three-year delay to first reproduction is an important life-history trait that allows individuals to acquire the foraging proficiency and body condition necessary to successfully incubate eggs and provision chicks. During these pre-breeding years, young terns engage in extensive prospecting behavior, visiting potential nesting sites and observing the foraging success of established breeders. The age at first reproduction is a critical demographic variable that influences population growth rates, and a delay of this magnitude is characteristic of species with high adult survival and low annual fecundity. This extended period of immaturity contrasts sharply with smaller tern species that may breed in their second calendar year, highlighting a strategy that trades early reproduction for enhanced survival and future reproductive potential.

The maximum adult body mass attained by Caspian terns is substantial, placing them among the heaviest of all tern species. The maximum wet weight recorded for the species is 644 grams [Wwi = 644 grams], which falls comfortably within the widely cited range of 530 to 782 grams for adult individuals. This considerable mass, coupled with a wingspan that can exceed 130 centimeters, supports a strong, powerful flight capable of long-distance migrations between breeding and wintering grounds. The species also exhibits an impressive maximum lifespan, with the oldest documented individuals reaching an age of 30 years [am = 30 years] at the typical metabolic temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This remarkable longevity, combined with a modest annual reproductive output, defines the slow end of the life-history continuum. Female Caspian terns produce a single clutch of two eggs per breeding season [Ri = two eggs per breeding season], and they typically attempt only one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year]. These parameters yield an annual reproductive output of approximately 2 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 2 eggs per year], a low fecundity that is compensated by high adult and juvenile survival rates, enabling populations to persist even in variable environments.
